newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl appeals to SPD over German tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Kohl appeals to SPD over German tax reform.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday appealed to the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to adopt a constructive stance in talks on plans for a major reform of Germany's tax system aimed at cutting record unemployment.

Kohl, who will head a delegation from his centre-right coalition at Monday's talks with the SPD, said in an interview released ahead of publication on Sunday that the government's tax reform plans were too important for political games.

"The tax reform is vital for Germany as an industrial location, to maintain our international competitiveness, as a motor for economic upturn but above all to secure existing jobs and cut unemployment," Kohl told the Welt am Sonntag weekly.

"Talks like these, between the coalition and the SPD, only make sense when everybody involved is ready to come to concrete results quickly. So there can't be any more party political showfights," he told the newspaper.

Shaken by January's half-million surge in unemployment to 4.7 million -- the highest figure since 1933 -- both sides have said they are ready to end a standoff and search for a quick deal to avert long and bitter wrangling in parliament.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax reform plans aim to cut 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion) in tax to boost jobs and ensure lasting fitness for European monetary union (EMU).
Kohl's coalition has enough support to get the plans through the lower house of parliament but will need SPD help to win approval in the upper chamber.
"I see the opportunity for us to send an important signal about the willingness and ability to reform in Germany," Kohl said.
Waigel's strategy plans a two-stage reform, with cuts in corporate taxes starting in 1998 and a drop in income tax in 1999. The cuts would be offset by scrapping 70 tax breaks.
